title: Epistolae [Incertus]
author: Maximus of Turin
source: Translated by Claude from tmp916.tmp916.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Quem talis cogitatio non cum admiratione delectet ? Reliquias, inquam, corporum nostrorum aut nullas aut minimas certe , et quantulascunque, attamen sordidas, et animi nunquam sine horrore inspectas in suum iterum hominem , non ut Pythagoras mentiens et delirans a in Euphorbo esse credatur, sed in proprium suum corpus, et nomen, per ossa et nervos, per venas, per cuncta vitalia, b verum etiam articulatim recompaginandum. Hoc autem non est angustum, cum omnium vel frugum vel stirpium semina, majora, et pulchriora in graminibus redeant, quam in terra vel ab hominibus sata sunt, vel sua sponte ceciderunt. c Quis non seminari se in terra, ut ita dixerim , lxtetur, quæ nos meliores quam acceperat reddat, dicente Apostolo : Reaurrectio mortuorum seminatur in corruptione; d surget autem in incorruptione (I Cor. xv). Quæ possessio præsentium huic spei poterit comparari ? Aut quid erit aliud, quod ad contemptum mortis attollat, quam haec meditatio divinis promissionibus et prophelarum vocibus explicata ?
passages.english: Whom would such a thought not delight, together with wonder? The remains, I say, of our bodies, either none or certainly very small, and however slight, yet filthy, and never looked upon without a shudder of the mind, [are] to be put back together again into their own man, not, as Pythagoras lying and raving [claimed], so that he might be believed to be in Euphorbus, but into its own proper body and name, through bones and sinews, through veins, through all the vital parts, indeed even joint by joint. Nor is this hard to grasp, since the seeds of all crops or plants come back larger and more beautiful in their shoots than they were when sown in the earth by men or fell there of their own accord. Who would not rejoice to be sown, so to speak, in the earth, which returns us better than it had received [us], as the Apostle says: "The resurrection of the dead is sown in corruption; but it will rise in incorruption" (1 Cor. 15)? What possession of present things could be compared with this hope? Or what else will there be to lift [us] up to contempt of death than this meditation, unfolded by the divine promises and the voices of the prophets?
passages.notes: Stray letters a, b, c, d are footnote marks and are omitted. 'lxtetur' read as 'laetetur', 'Reaurrectio' as 'Resurrectio', 'prophelarum' as 'prophetarum'. The first long sentence has no finite main verb; 'recompaginandum' (to be put back together) is taken as governing it. The scriptural quotation is a loose citation of 1 Cor. 15:42.

passages.original: Quid hi facient, qui tanquam correptores morum, Domini familiam attentius castigatiusque viventem, d aut in ve- stibus humili colore, aut in cibi arida parcitate, aut in vigiliarum non otiosa sobrietate, velut aut indumentis mollioribus dclicatam,autepulis copiosioribus saginatam, aut thoris calidioribus oscitantem divellunt ac vexant, nescientes quod in sanctis Dei martyribus confessoribusque oculi ejus pupilla feriatur? Peribunl sine dubio, peribunt in illa die omnes cogitationes eorum: nec eos apud tribunal illud aut Lu. cius Crassus defendet, aut M. Antonius, aut istis eloquentior Tullius : quoniam omnis tunc sæculi lingua obmutescet, et sola erit in rusticulis suis facunda iu- stitia, quæ infantium fecit ora diserta, et mutorum linguas novum solvit in canticum, coelestemque sibi harmoniam per sui misericordiam de suis oviculis acquisivit.
passages.english: What will these men do who, as though they were correctors of morals, tear apart and harass the Lord's household, which lives more attentively and more strictly, whether in garments of humble colour, or in the dry sparseness of its food, or in the unidle sobriety of its vigils, as if it were made delicate by softer clothing, or fattened by more abundant feasts, or yawning on warmer beds, not knowing that in God's holy martyrs and confessors the pupil of his eye is struck? They will perish without doubt; all their thoughts will perish on that day. Nor will Lucius Crassus defend them before that tribunal, or Marcus Antonius, or Tullius, more eloquent than these: for then every tongue of the world will fall silent, and justice alone will be eloquent in her rustic folk, she who made the mouths of infants articulate, and loosed the tongues of the mute into a new song, and through her mercy gained for herself a heavenly harmony from her little sheep.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently ('dclicatam', 'Peribunl', 'Lu. cius', 'iu- stitia'); stray 'd' omitted. 'Tullius' is Cicero. The rendering of 'Domini familiam ... velut ... delicatam' as an accusation (as if they were pampered) is an interpretation; the syntax is somewhat loose.

passages.original: Et quia et ipsi dæmones operantur, intelligere naturas, quæ 147 vera sunt, quæ falsa, quæ novisse, est, non decipi, non errare-, non inimico assignare quae Dei sunt, nec Deo adjudicare quæ sunt dæmonum, scire tempora, signa cognoscere, habere Domini cognitam voluntatem : et alia Dei mirabilia cum gratiarum actione venerari, alia cum digna exsecratione vitare. Talem virum etiam saeculi homines laudavere, dicente Virgilio Felix qui potuit reram cogooscere causas. Bona sententia, si ad eam suo itinere venisset, ut appareat illum ignorasse b quod laudat : primis omissis, quæ sunt secunda celebravit. Nam et ordinc praepostero etiam sapientis vertit officium : dum non rerum causæ, sed rerum Creator inquirendus est, per quem ad causas rerum, si ipsum didicerimus, intrabimus.
passages.english: And since the demons too work [wonders], [it is something] to understand natures: which are true, which false, which [it is] to know, that is, not to be deceived, not to err, not to assign to the enemy what belongs to God, nor to award to God what belongs to demons; to know the times, to recognize the signs, to have the Lord's will known; and to venerate some of God's wonders with thanksgiving, and to shun others with fitting execration. Even men of the world have praised such a man, as Virgil says: "Happy he who was able to know the causes of things." A good sentiment, if he had come to it by its proper road, but so that it appears he did not know what he praises: leaving out the first things, he celebrated those that are second. For in reversed order he even overturns the duty of the wise man: since it is not the causes of things but the Creator of things who must be sought, through whom, if we have learned him, we shall enter into the causes of things.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is syntactically obscure and probably corrupt ('quæ novisse, est' especially); the translation is tentative and may continue the infinitives ('distinguere...') of the preceding context. '147' is a page number, 'b' a footnote mark; 'reram cogooscere' read as 'rerum cognoscere', 'ordinc' as 'ordine'. Quotation is Virgil, Georgics 2.490.
